# A Foreign Country with a Smell

L. P. Hartley wrote that the past is a foreign country: they do things differently there. True, but incomplete. Customs are the least of it. Drop back six or seven hundred years and the first disorientation would not be architectural or linguistic. It would arrive through senses you barely knew you had.

Begin with the air. Every medieval town ran on animals. Oxen hauled, horses carried, pigs rooted through lanes that doubled as sewers, chickens scurried underfoot, sheep funneled toward market, and dogs performed whatever jobs dogs perform in cities without police or exterminators. Beneath the hooves, dung was trampled into paste by ten thousand feet. Along the gutters ran the urine that some households saved and sold to tanners and dyers, who needed its ammonia. Butchers worked in the open air. At the edges of town rose the middens. And floating above all of it, permanently, woodsmoke—because every meal of every life was cooked over fire, every ceiling was stained black above the hearth, and every woolen cloak carried, faintly but indelibly, the smell of the room where it dried. You would gag for a week. Then your nose would shut down, exactly as theirs had, and you would stop noticing, which is somehow worse.

We dress the Middle Ages in sepia, partly because movies like mood lighting and partly because the objects that survived deceive us. Stone, oak, and vellum last; the pigment on a stone saint eventually flakes off while his painted cousin in an illuminated manuscript stays vermilion forever. It is a cruel accident of preservation. In their own day the statues were flesh-toned and gold-crowned, church interiors so densely colored they must have resembled the insides of jeweled boxes, and the streets ran bright with dyed cloth: woad blue, madder red, weld yellow, scarlet wrung at extravagant cost from thousands of crushed kermes insects. Gaudiness was the norm. Beige had not been invented.

Yet while the past was more colorful than we imagine, it was also darker than we can easily conceive. Indoors meant flame: tallow candles if you were rich, rushlights if you were poor, firelight shading between. Outdoors, after sunset, night fell absolutely. No glow puckered the undersides of clouds. Nothing stood between a village and the universe but air. It is usually said, correctly, that almost nobody alive today sees the Milky Way from a major city; it is less often noted that in 1350 almost nobody failed to. It was not a destination requiring a holiday in a certified dark-sky reserve. It was the ceiling. Peasants who never left their county knew the heavens the way commuters know a timetable.

Subtract the engine—all engines—and the soundscape becomes equally unrecognizable: long silences of a purity we reserve for recording studios, punctuated by sound traveling improbable distances. Bells were the infrastructure. They woke the town, warned of fire, measured the working day, and called the curfew, a word that began life as *couvre-feu*, "cover the fire," the signal to bank your hearth and sit in the dark. News, meanwhile, arrived in shouting mouths. A crier declaimed proclamations, fines, and occasionally your misdeeds to whoever cared to gather. Reputation was broadcast live. Gossip had physics.

Even sleep wore a different shape. Sifting centuries of diaries, court records, and medical texts, the historian Roger Ekirch found candid references to "first sleep" and "second sleep," mentioned as casually as we mention lunch. People retired shortly after dark, slept hard for a few hours, then woke naturally near midnight into a calm, purposeful wakefulness: some prayed, some read, some talked or visited neighbors, some tended embers, couples enjoyed the privacy that nighttime uniquely afforded. Only then came the second sleep, running on to dawn. The electric lamp welded those two segments into a single block, and now, whenever the old midnight waking resurfaces—as it does for many—the phenomenon is filed under a diagnosis. Insomnia. As though an ancient rhythm were a malfunction of modern wiring.

Consider, too, the mirror. Clear, flat, affordable glass mirrors are startlingly recent, a Venetian specialty of the sixteenth century; before that, polished metal offered a smeared ghost, and for most people across most of history the sharpest available portrait was a bucket of still water. Whole lives unfolded in which no one ever clearly saw their own face. Whatever the self was, it could not be maintained by inspection. It lived in what others bounced back: in the temperature of greetings, in whether a room went quieter when you entered, in the slow accumulation of name. We have inverted the arrangement entirely. Cameras ride in our pockets, lenses face us at arm's length, our voices return to us recorded. We cannot stop looking at ourselves. Whether that counts as progress or merely a subtler kind of blindness is a question that would never have occurred to them and quietly obsesses us.

All of this suggests something disquieting about how history gets written. Documents preserve arguments, transactions, creeds—the declarative layer of a civilization. They almost never record the substrate: the smoke, the bells, the mid-dark sky, the smell of the lane after rain. Nobody describes the water they swim in. Which points to the second, larger implication—if the texture of the past was invisible to its own inhabitants, ours is invisible to us. Some visitor from seven hundred years forward would stagger past our monuments to gawk at our particulars: the low drone of machines cooling in windowless rooms, screens pouring artificial noon onto faces at 3 a.m., aircraft stitching the stratosphere, and a social invention no previous century could have parsed—crowded cafés where everyone sits sealed in private audio, together yet utterly elsewhere.

They would find us alien in ways we cannot report, because reporting requires noticing. The past is a foreign country, Hartley said, and he was right. But so is the present. The only difference is that the present is the one foreign country we are denied entry to as tourists—we were born citizens, and citizenship here means never quite smelling the air.

Actually, let me consider writing about something that combines intellectual curiosity with beautiful prose. What about an essay on "the loss of night"—light pollution and what we've lost astronomically? That's evocative. Or the history of forgetting before writing?

Let me think about what makes free writing good: voice, specificity, surprise, movement. It should have momentum—a sense that each paragraph earns the next.

I'm drawn to writing about the medieval sensorium—the idea that people in the past lived in worlds that smelled, sounded, and looked radically different from ours. There's great material here: 
- Churches that were painted in brilliant colors (we think of them as gray stone)
- Statues were painted—the Greeks and Romans painted their marble
- Cities smelled of animals, dung, smoke, tanneries, spices
- Soundscapes: church bells marking hours, criers, no ambient mechanical hum
- Darkness was real darkness after sunset
- People slept in two shifts—"first sleep" and "second sleep" with a waking period between (Roger Ekirch's research)
- Spices weren't to mask rotten meat (myth) but status display
- Bread as the caloric backbone
- The absence of mirrors for most people—most people had never clearly seen their own face except in water or bad mirrors
- Colors had different meanings; purple dye from murex snails
- Time wasn't clock-time but season/task-time ("task orientation" per E.P. Thompson)

That's a rich vein. The two-sleep thing is fascinating and well documented. The mirrors point is genuinely startling—we are perhaps the first generation saturated with self-images.

Alternatively: an essay about time perception—proportional theory (a year at age 5 is 20% of your life), novelty density, the reminiscence bump, why we remember vacations in snapshots. Also nice.

Or the deep sea essay: more people have been to the Moon than the deepest trenches; barreleye fish with transparent heads; the ocean's midnight zone; marine snow; whale fall ecosystems.

Let me go with the medieval/past sensorium essay but give it a personal, reflective frame—not as a lecture but as a meditation on how the past isn't just different in beliefs but in texture—that history is not just ideas changing but the very feel of days changing. The hook: we imagine time travel would show us same world, different clothes—but actually you'd be stranded in an alien sensorium. The colors wrong, the soundscape unrecognizable, darkness absolute, smells overwhelming.

Structure sketch (~1000 words):
1. Opening: The fantasy of time travel assumes the past looks basically like now minus technology. But step into a medieval town and the first shock wouldn't be architecture—it'd be your eyes watering. Smell: ungathered refuse, animal dung (cities full of horses, pigs, chickens), smoke from wood fires permeating everything—clothes, hair, food cooked over fire tastes smoky.
2. Color and light: We imagine the past in sepia. Wrong—churches blazed with pigment; statues painted lifelike; clothes dyed woad, madder, weld. What faded was the medium, not the message. Conversely, candlelit interiors, and true night outside—no orange glow, the Milky Way as ordinary furniture of the sky. Most people saw stars we need planetariums to approximate.
3. Sound: No engines—so sudden silence or sudden loudness. Bells structuring time; streets announced by criers. Your name might be spoken by a town official announcing fines.
4. Sleep: Segmented sleep—first sleep, the watchful interval ("the watch"), second sleep. Documents reference it casually—people prayed, chatted, did chores. Electric light compressed this into one monolithic block, and we call the old pattern insomnia.
5. Faces and selves: Few mirrors—most went life without seeing themselves clearly. Selfhood anchored differently—in how others mirrored you, in reputation. Now we're flooded with self-image; curating avatars.
6. Close: The lesson—history isn't only a sequence of events but a sequence of textures. And it implies the present too is just a texture—we can't see our own strangeness, because we're soaked in it. Future time travelers would find our world equally alien—our fluorescent hums, blue-lit screens, our characteristic silence of empty public spaces now everyone wears earbuds. The most alien place might be our own moment, seen from outside.

That structure has a real arc ending on a reflective turn. Good.

Facts to verify/keep accurate-ish:
- Polychromy of Greek/Roman/medieval statuary: well-documented. Medieval churches were brightly painted inside—true (e.g., St. Mary's Church Lübeck reconstructions, Chartres originally vivid).
- Dyes: woad (blue), madder (red), weld (yellow), kermes/cochineal for scarlets (kermes in medieval Europe), Tyrian purple from murex earlier.
- Horses in cities: New York 1900 ~100,000-200,000 horses. Medieval cities similarly animal-dense. Mainz estimate, London. I'll speak generally.
- Woodsmoke indoors: everyone cooked over wood/peat; soot darkened ceilings.
- Segmented sleep: Roger Ekirch, "At Day's Close" — "first sleep," "morning watch"/"dread" — widely cited. Terms: "firste slepe," people woke for prayer, reflection, sex, visits. I'll describe generally without overclaiming specific phrases... though "first sleep" is attested. Safe.
- Mirrors: flat glass mirrors poor until 16th century Venice; metal mirrors (speculum) dim; most peasants rarely saw accurate reflections. Reasonable claim with hedging.
- Milky Way visible pre-light-pollution: yes.
- Church bells as time: yes; clocks arrived late 13th-14th centuries in towers; even then bells rang.
- Curfew literally "cover-fire" (couvre-feu): bell signaling fire cover—nice detail, true etymology.

Now word count: aim near 1000 words. I'll write flowing prose, minimal headers (maybe none—an essay reads better continuous). Free writing invites essay form. Keep paragraphs moderately sized. Let me draft mentally with attention to rhythm.

L.P. Hartley wrote that the past is a foreign country; they do things differently there. What he didn't say—and what we keep forgetting—is that it isn't just customs that differ. What no film has ever replicated is the moment the wind changed direction.

**A Foreign Country with a Smell**

L.P. Hartley wrote that the past is a foreign country; they do things differently there. What he didn't say—and what we keep forgetting—is that it isn't just customs that differ. It's the light, the sound, the air itself. If you dropped into a European town of, say, 1350, the clothing and the cathedral would strike you, sure, but those are images you've seen in films. What no film has ever replicated is the moment the wind changed direction.

Then paragraph on smell: Every town ran on animals—horses, oxen, pigs in the street, chickens, sheep driven through for market, dogs everywhere. Dung piled along gutters, urine collected for tanning and dyeing (true: piss used in fulling/tanning). Butchering happened in the open. Refuse heaped at edges. Over it all, smoke: nearly every meal anyone ate had been cooked over wood, every interior stained by soot, every garment smelling faintly of the hearth. You'd gag for a week and then go noseblind—as everyone then had done.

Color paragraph: We picture the Middle Ages in sepia because the things that survived to us—stone, parchment—have faded. But carved saints were painted garish-lifelike, churches' interiors covered in pigment, streets full of dyed cloth—woad blue, madder red, weld yellow; scarlet from crushed kermis insects costing fortunes. Gaudy was normal; beige was nonexistent. Meanwhile in another sense the world was darker: indoor life meant candles and rushlights, and outdoors, once the sun set, night fell for real. No sodium glow on cloud bases. The Milky Way wasn't special—it was furniture. Peasants who never traveled knew the sky better than most astronomers today.

Sound paragraph: subtract engines. Sudden noises, long silences. Bells as infrastructure—they rang workers up, warned of fire, marked curfew—which literally means "cover fire," the signal to bank your hearth. Town criers shouted news/laws—your reputation could be amplified by someone paid to shout your misdeeds.

Sleep paragraph: Ekirch's segmented sleep. First sleep, then a quiet hour or two awake around midnight—prayer, conversation, small chores, intimacy—then second sleep until dawn. Diaries refer casually, as normal. Electric light welded the two segments into one. Now we name it insomnia/disorder—perhaps it's older pattern surfacing.

Mirrors paragraph: Glass mirrors, clear and flat, cheap enough — essentially post-16th-century Venetian tech; before that polished metal gave vague reflections; most people's clearest self-portrait was still water. Whole lives led without ever really seeing your own face. The self was housed differently—located in the reactions of others, memory, reputation—rather than in self-inspection. Compare us: cameras everywhere, selfies, video calls—we can't stop seeing ourselves. Different self-tech, different self.

Closing turn: This should change how we read all history: documents record beliefs/events but leave out the vast unstated baseline—the texture. Which raises uncomfortable thought: we too are marinated in a texture invisible to ourselves—the hum of refrigeration, the blue-white cast of screens, the smell of asphalt after rain, elevators, planes overhead, private silence of earbuds—public spaces full of people individually sealed away. A traveler from 700 years hence would be floored by details we don't know we have. The truly alien country may be now—we merely lack the sensorium to perceive it as foreign.
